topics.title: Couinaud Liver Segments
topics.frontClue: Hepatic veins split the liver side to side; portal veins split it top from bottom
topics.corePiece: The Couinaud system divides the liver into eight functionally independent segments. The three hepatic veins run between segments (interlobar and intersegmental) and divide the liver longitudinally; the right and left portal veins run within segments (intrasegmental) and divide it into superior and inferior tiers. Segment 1 is the caudate lobe, which drains directly into the IVC. Segments 2 (superior) and 3 (inferior) form the left lateral section; segment 4 (4a superior, 4b inferior) is the left medial section. On the right, segments 5 and 8 form the anterior section, and 6 and 7 form the posterior section, with the lower number inferior. The middle hepatic vein and the main lobar fissure, which points to the gallbladder fossa, separate the right and left lobes. The left hepatic vein and the ligamentum teres separate left medial from left lateral. A normal liver measures about 15 to 15.5 cm or less in the midclavicular line, with echogenicity equal to or slightly greater than the right renal cortex.
topics.whyLock: Segment location is how surgeons and radiologists report lesions, so you must translate a described position into a segment number. Remember the numbering runs clockwise from the caudate when viewed from the front, and that within each section the lower number sits inferiorly. Traps: portal veins are intrasegmental, not intersegmental; the falciform ligament and ligamentum teres split the left lobe, not right from left. The caudate's separate venous drainage explains why it is spared and enlarges in Budd-Chiari syndrome and cirrhosis. A Riedel lobe is a normal tongue-like extension of the right lobe, not hepatomegaly.

topics.title: Diffuse Liver Disease
topics.frontClue: Bright liver, dark liver, nodular liver: fat, acute hepatitis, cirrhosis
topics.corePiece: Fatty infiltration (steatosis) raises liver echogenicity well above the renal cortex, attenuates the beam so the deep liver and diaphragm become hard to see, and blurs the portal vein walls. It can be diffuse, focal, or diffuse with focal sparing; spared areas and focal fat favor the gallbladder fossa, the area anterior to the portal bifurcation, and the caudate lobe, and they show no mass effect and vessels running through them undisplaced. Common causes include obesity, diabetes, alcohol, and steroids. Acute hepatitis may look normal, or the parenchyma may become hypoechoic so that portal triad walls look bright (starry sky), often with gallbladder wall thickening and hepatomegaly. Chronic hepatitis coarsens the echotexture. Cirrhosis shows a nodular surface (best seen with a high-frequency linear probe), coarse heterogeneous parenchyma, atrophy of the right lobe with hypertrophy of the caudate and left lateral segments (caudate to right lobe width ratio above about 0.65), and signs of portal hypertension. Hepatic venous waveforms may lose their normal triphasic pattern and become flat.
topics.whyLock: Pattern recognition is the key skill. A bright, poorly penetrated liver is fat until proven otherwise, but cirrhosis can also look bright, so the surface contour, caudate size, and portal hypertension signs separate them. Do not mistake focal sparing for a hypoechoic mass: look for its typical location, geographic margins, and absence of vessel displacement. Every cirrhotic liver is surveyed for hepatocellular carcinoma, so any new solid nodule matters. Trap: starry sky belongs to acute hepatitis, not to fatty liver, which causes the opposite effect of hiding portal walls.

topics.title: Benign Liver Masses
topics.frontClue: Bright hemangioma, stealthy FNH with a scar, bleeding adenoma on the pill
topics.corePiece: Hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor: a well-defined, homogeneously hyperechoic mass, usually under 3 cm and often subcapsular in the right lobe, with possible posterior enhancement and little detectable internal color flow. Larger ones become heterogeneous. On contrast imaging it shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in. Focal nodular hyperplasia, the second most common benign tumor, is typically seen in women and is often nearly isoechoic to liver (a stealth lesion) with a central scar and spoke-wheel arterial flow radiating from a central artery. Hepatic adenoma occurs in women on oral contraceptives, anabolic steroid users, and glycogen storage disease type I; it is variable in echogenicity and its main danger is hemorrhage and rare malignant transformation, so it is usually resected. A simple hepatic cyst is anechoic and thin walled, with posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal flow or contrast enhancement. Pyogenic abscess is complex with debris and possibly gas; amebic abscess is round, hypoechoic, and peripheral near the diaphragm after travel. Echinococcal (hydatid) cysts show daughter cysts or a floating membrane (water lily sign).
topics.whyLock: The exam pairs each mass with a hallmark: hemangioma with hyperechoic and centripetal fill-in, FNH with central scar and spoke-wheel flow, adenoma with oral contraceptives and bleeding. Clinical context separates infections: fever and high white count suggest abscess; travel or exposure to sheep and dogs suggests amebic or hydatid disease. Trap: in a fatty liver, a hemangioma may appear relatively hypoechoic because the background is brighter. Trap two: a hyperechoic lesion in a cirrhotic patient or a cancer patient cannot be assumed to be a hemangioma, because some HCCs and colon metastases are echogenic.

topics.title: Malignant Liver Lesions
topics.frontClue: Cirrhosis plus rising AFP: think HCC; multiple targets: think metastases
topics.corePiece: Metastases are the most common malignant liver lesions, far outnumbering primary tumors. They are usually multiple and variable: hyperechoic metastases suggest colon, renal cell, or carcinoid primaries; hypoechoic ones suggest breast, lung, or lymphoma; a target or bull's-eye pattern with a hypoechoic halo is a classic appearance; calcified metastases suggest mucinous colon cancer; cystic ones suggest necrosis or cystic primaries. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver malignancy and arises mostly in cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis B or C. It may be solitary, multifocal, or diffusely infiltrative, with variable echogenicity; small lesions are often hypoechoic. Alpha-fetoprotein is frequently elevated. HCC tends to invade the portal vein; tumor thrombus expands the vein and shows arterial-type flow within the thrombus, unlike bland thrombus. Cholangiocarcinoma and hepatoblastoma (young children) are other primaries. Fibrolamellar HCC affects young adults without cirrhosis and has a central scar.
topics.whyLock: Reason from the clinical history. A known primary plus multiple lesions means metastases; cirrhosis or hepatitis B plus a new nodule and rising AFP means HCC until proven otherwise. The single most testable Doppler fact is that tumor thrombus contains arterial flow while bland thrombus does not. Trap: HCC can be hyperechoic and mimic hemangioma, so a bright lesion in a cirrhotic liver needs further characterization. Trap two: a target appearance in the liver is a hallmark of metastasis, whereas a target in the bowel usually means wall thickening.

topics.title: Portal Hypertension and TIPS
topics.frontClue: When the liver blocks the road, flow reverses and finds collaterals
topics.corePiece: Normal main portal vein flow is hepatopetal (toward the liver), gently phasic with respiration, at roughly 15 to 40 cm/s, and the vein is usually 13 mm or less in diameter. Portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis, causes a portal vein over 13 mm with lost respiratory variation, slow or to-and-fro flow, and eventually hepatofugal flow. Other signs are splenomegaly, ascites, and portosystemic collaterals: the coronary (left gastric) vein toward esophageal varices, a recanalized paraumbilical vein in the ligamentum teres, splenorenal and short gastric collaterals. Cavernous transformation is a web of collaterals replacing a chronically occluded vein. A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) connects, usually, the right portal vein to the right hepatic vein. With a working TIPS, main portal velocity rises and flow in the intrahepatic portal branches reverses toward the shunt. Commonly cited shunt velocities are about 90 to 190 cm/s; values outside that range, a change of more than 50 cm/s from baseline, or a return to hepatopetal flow in the portal branches suggest dysfunction.
topics.whyLock: Think of portal hypertension as pressure seeking an escape route. Hepatofugal flow and collaterals mean the pressure is high enough to push blood away from the liver. For TIPS, the trap is reversed flow in the left and right portal branches: after TIPS that is expected and healthy, because blood now runs into the low-resistance shunt. Reversion to hepatopetal branch flow is the warning sign. Exact TIPS thresholds vary between institutions, so focus on the trend from the baseline study and on absent flow, which means occlusion.

topics.title: Liver Transplant Doppler
topics.frontClue: In a new liver, the hepatic artery is the lifeline: lose it and the bile ducts die
topics.corePiece: The transplanted liver depends on the hepatic artery for biliary blood supply, so hepatic artery thrombosis is the most serious vascular complication, typically early, and it can lead to biliary necrosis, bile leak, and graft loss. Doppler shows absent arterial flow at the porta hepatis and in the liver. Hepatic artery stenosis, usually at the anastomosis, produces a focal velocity elevation (often above about 200 cm/s) with turbulence, and a tardus parvus waveform downstream: slow systolic upstroke, acceleration time over about 0.08 s, and resistive index below 0.5. A normal post-transplant hepatic arterial RI is roughly 0.5 to 0.8; a transiently high RI in the first days is common and usually resolves. Portal vein stenosis or thrombosis, and IVC or hepatic venous anastomotic stenosis, are the other vascular complications. Fluid collections include hematoma, biloma, seroma, and abscess. Rejection has no reliable sonographic sign and is diagnosed by biopsy.
topics.whyLock: Organize transplant Doppler by vessel: artery, portal vein, hepatic veins and IVC. The artery is tested most because its failure threatens the bile ducts. Tardus parvus is the downstream fingerprint of a proximal stenosis, so a low RI with a slow upstroke is more worrying than a high RI. Trap: collateral arteries can develop after thrombosis and produce a weak tardus parvus signal, so faint intrahepatic flow does not exclude a thrombosed main artery. Trap two: do not expect ultrasound to diagnose rejection.

topics.title: Normal Biliary Anatomy
topics.frontClue: Fast for the gallbladder; measure the duct inner wall to inner wall
topics.corePiece: After a fast of about 6 to 8 hours in adults, the gallbladder is distended, anechoic, and pear shaped, typically up to about 8 to 10 cm long and 4 to 5 cm wide, with a wall of 3 mm or less measured on the anterior wall perpendicular to the beam. It has a fundus, body, neck, and Hartmann pouch; a Phrygian cap is a normal fundal fold. The cystic duct, with its spiral valves of Heister, joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct. The common duct lies anterior and lateral to the main portal vein and anterior to the right hepatic artery in the porta hepatis (Mickey Mouse sign), then runs posterolateral in the pancreatic head. Normal common duct diameter is about 6 mm or less, commonly allowing roughly 1 mm more per decade over age 60, and up to about 10 mm after cholecystectomy. Intrahepatic ducts are normally 2 mm or less, or under 40 percent of the adjacent portal vein diameter.
topics.whyLock: Normal values are the yardstick for every biliary question. Measure the duct inner wall to inner wall at its widest point. Use more than one patient position, such as left lateral decubitus and upright, to move stones and resolve folds. Traps: a nonfasting patient has a contracted gallbladder with an apparently thick wall, so check prep before calling wall thickening. A Phrygian cap is a normal variant, not a septum or mass. Age and prior cholecystectomy raise the upper limit for the common duct, so judge dilation in context.

topics.title: Gallstones and Sludge
topics.frontClue: Bright, mobile and shadowing is a stone; layering without a shadow is sludge
topics.corePiece: Cholelithiasis is the most common gallbladder disease, with risk factors classically summarized as female, fat, forty, and fertile, plus pregnancy, rapid weight loss, and hemolytic disorders. A typical stone is echogenic, casts a clean posterior acoustic shadow, and moves to the dependent wall when the patient changes position. Shadowing is improved by placing the focal zone at the stone, using a higher frequency, and using harmonic imaging; very small stones may not shadow. A gallbladder packed with stones may show the wall-echo-shadow (WES) sign: the anterior wall, the bright stone surface, then shadow. A stone impacted in the neck does not move and may cause obstruction. Sludge consists of low-level echoes without shadowing that layer dependently and move slowly; it occurs with fasting, total parenteral nutrition, critical illness, and pregnancy. Tumefactive sludge (a sludge ball) can mimic a polyp or mass but has no internal color flow and changes shape or position over time.
topics.whyLock: Mobility and shadowing are the two questions to ask of any echogenic gallbladder focus. Mobile and shadowing equals stone; fixed and nonshadowing suggests a polyp; layering low-level echoes suggest sludge. The WES sign can be confused with bowel gas in the gallbladder fossa; the wall echo in front of the shadow is the clue. Traps: a fold can cast a refraction shadow, and gas in bowel produces a dirty rather than clean shadow. Emphysematous cholecystitis and porcelain gallbladder also cause shadowing from the wall itself.

topics.title: Acute Cholecystitis
topics.frontClue: Stones plus a positive sonographic Murphy sign: the strongest combination
topics.corePiece: Acute cholecystitis usually results from a stone obstructing the gallbladder neck or cystic duct. Patients have right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. The two most predictive findings are gallstones and a positive sonographic Murphy sign, meaning maximal tenderness when the transducer presses directly over the gallbladder; together they carry a high positive predictive value. Supporting findings include wall thickening over 3 mm, often with a striated or hypoechoic layered wall, pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder distension, an impacted stone, and wall hyperemia. Complications include gangrenous cholecystitis, with asymmetric wall thickening, intraluminal membranes, and a Murphy sign that may be absent because of nerve necrosis; emphysematous cholecystitis, with gas in the wall or lumen producing bright echoes and dirty shadowing or ring-down, more common in diabetics; and perforation, with a wall defect and pericholecystic abscess. Acalculous cholecystitis affects critically ill patients such as those in intensive care or after trauma or burns. Chronic cholecystitis shows a small, contracted, thick-walled gallbladder with stones.
topics.whyLock: Wall thickening alone is nonspecific: hepatitis, ascites, heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, and a postprandial state all thicken the wall. That is why stones and a focal Murphy sign carry more weight. Always perform the Murphy sign yourself before the patient gets pain medication, because analgesia blunts it. Trap: a negative Murphy sign does not exclude disease if the gallbladder is gangrenous. Trap two: gas in the wall can be mistaken for a porcelain gallbladder or bowel; ring-down artifact and clinical toxicity point to emphysematous cholecystitis, a surgical emergency.

topics.title: Gallbladder Wall Lesions
topics.frontClue: Comet tails mean adenomyomatosis; fixed, nonshadowing bumps are polyps
topics.corePiece: Adenomyomatosis is a benign hyperplastic condition in which mucosa herniates into a thickened muscular wall, forming Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses. Cholesterol crystals in these sinuses create bright foci with V-shaped comet-tail reverberation artifact on gray scale and often twinkling artifact on color Doppler. It may be diffuse, segmental (hourglass narrowing), or focal at the fundus. Gallbladder polyps are fixed, nonshadowing, nonmobile projections from the wall; most are cholesterol polyps, and they may show a small feeding vessel. Size and shape drive management. The classic teaching is surgical referral at 10 mm or larger. The 2022 SRU consensus stratifies by morphology: extremely low risk polyps (pedunculated ball-on-the-wall or thin stalk) need no follow-up up to 9 mm, ultrasound follow-up at 6, 12 and 24 months for 10 to 14 mm, and surgical consultation at 15 mm or more; low risk polyps (sessile or broad-based) need no follow-up up to 6 mm, follow-up at 12 months for 7 to 9 mm, follow-up or surgical consultation for 10 to 14 mm, and surgical consultation at 15 mm or more. Adjacent focal wall thickening of 4 mm or more, or growth of 4 mm or more within 12 months, prompts surgical consultation. Gallbladder carcinoma is associated with gallstones, chronic inflammation, and porcelain gallbladder (wall calcification). It appears as a mass replacing the gallbladder lumen, focal or diffuse irregular wall thickening, or an intraluminal mass with internal flow, often invading the adjacent liver and causing biliary obstruction at the porta hepatis.
topics.whyLock: The two key separations are polyp versus stone (fixed and nonshadowing versus mobile and shadowing) and polyp versus tumefactive sludge (internal flow and fixed position versus avascular and shifting). Comet-tail artifact from the wall is reassuring because it signals adenomyomatosis. Exact polyp follow-up thresholds have changed with recent consensus, so learn the classic 10 mm rule while recognizing that morphology now matters. Trap: a porcelain gallbladder can look like a stone-filled gallbladder because of the curvilinear shadowing wall, and both carry different implications for cancer risk.

topics.title: Biliary Obstruction
topics.frontClue: Find where the ducts stop dilating: that is where the problem lives
topics.corePiece: Obstructive jaundice raises direct (conjugated) bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT. Dilated intrahepatic ducts run parallel to portal veins, producing the parallel channel (shotgun) sign. The level of obstruction is found where dilated ducts become normal. Choledocholithiasis is the most common cause; distal duct stones may lack shadowing and are often obscured by duodenal gas. Distal obstruction from a pancreatic head or ampullary mass dilates both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct (double-duct sign); Courvoisier sign is a painless, palpable, nontender enlarged gallbladder with jaundice, suggesting malignant obstruction rather than stone disease. Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor) dilates intrahepatic ducts that fail to join at the confluence, with a normal-caliber common duct. Mirizzi syndrome is a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compressing the common hepatic duct, dilating ducts above it with a normal duct below. A choledochal cyst, most commonly Todani type I fusiform dilation of the common duct, is a congenital cyst separate from the gallbladder, usually found in children.
topics.whyLock: Localizing obstruction is the reasoning skill being tested. Dilated intrahepatic ducts with a normal common duct point to the hilum (Klatskin or Mirizzi); dilated common and pancreatic ducts point to the pancreatic head or ampulla. Painless jaundice with a big gallbladder suggests cancer; painful jaundice with a small gallbladder suggests stones, since chronic inflammation prevents distension. Trap: dilated ducts can mimic vessels, so always use color Doppler. Trap two: a choledochal cyst can be mistaken for a duodenal or pancreatic cyst unless you show it communicating with the ducts.

topics.title: Pancreatic Anatomy
topics.frontClue: Find the splenic vein and you have found the back of the pancreas
topics.corePiece: The pancreas is a retroperitoneal gland lying in the anterior pararenal space, identified mainly by its vascular landmarks. The splenic vein runs along the posterior body and tail and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal confluence. The head sits in the duodenal C-loop, to the right of the SMV and anterior to the IVC; the uncinate process tucks posterior to the SMV. The neck lies anterior to the SMV and portal confluence, the body anterior to the SMA and aorta, and the tail extends toward the splenic hilum. The gastroduodenal artery marks the anterolateral head and the common bile duct the posterolateral head. Approximate upper limits are 3 cm for the head and 2.5 cm for the body and tail, with a main duct (duct of Wirsung) of about 3 mm or less. Echogenicity increases with age as fat replaces tissue: the gland is relatively hypoechoic in children and equal to or more echogenic than the liver in adults.
topics.whyLock: Most pancreatic questions are really vascular landmark questions. Learn the transverse picture: SMV to the left of the head, SMA behind the SMV, aorta behind the SMA, IVC behind the head. The GDA is anterior and the CBD posterior in the head, an easy pair to reverse under pressure. Trap: an echogenic pancreas in an older adult is usually normal fatty replacement, not chronic pancreatitis. Trap two: the splenic vein marks the posterior border of the body and tail; peripancreatic fluid tracking between the gland and the splenic vein lies in the anterior pararenal space, whereas fluid anterior to the pancreas, behind the stomach, is in the lesser sac. Fill the stomach with water to improve the window.

topics.title: Acute Pancreatitis
topics.frontClue: Gallstones and alcohol light the fire; lipase confirms it
topics.corePiece: Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory process most often caused by gallstones or alcohol; other causes include hypertriglyceridemia, trauma, ERCP, drugs, and hypercalcemia. Patients present with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting, with elevated serum amylase and lipase; lipase stays elevated longer and is more specific. The pancreas may look normal in mild disease. Otherwise it is diffusely enlarged and hypoechoic from edema, with poorly defined margins and peripancreatic fluid, often in the lesser sac and anterior pararenal space. Focal pancreatitis can mimic a mass. The main role of ultrasound is to look for gallstones and biliary dilation, which change management, because CT better stages severity. Under the revised Atlanta classification, early collections are acute peripancreatic fluid collections or acute necrotic collections; after about four weeks, they become a pseudocyst or walled-off necrosis. Vascular complications include splenic vein thrombosis and splenic artery pseudoaneurysm, which shows swirling yin-yang color flow inside a cystic-appearing mass.
topics.whyLock: The exam expects you to know that a normal-looking pancreas does not exclude pancreatitis, and that finding gallstones is the most important sonographic contribution. Bowel gas from ileus often limits the exam, so expect a suboptimal window. Trap: never assume a cystic mass near an inflamed pancreas is a simple pseudocyst; check it with color Doppler first, because a pseudoaneurysm looks cystic in gray scale and needle drainage would be dangerous. Trap two: amylase rises and falls quickly, so a late presentation may show only an elevated lipase.

topics.title: Chronic Pancreatitis and Pseudocyst
topics.frontClue: Calcified, shrunken and beaded: years of alcohol written in the gland
topics.corePiece: Chronic pancreatitis results from repeated inflammation, most often from alcohol, causing irreversible fibrosis and loss of exocrine and endocrine function, with chronic pain, malabsorption and steatorrhea, and diabetes. Sonographically the gland is small, heterogeneous, and echogenic with irregular margins. Parenchymal and intraductal calcifications are the most specific finding and may shadow. The main pancreatic duct is dilated and beaded or irregular, sometimes containing stones. Pseudocysts are common, and the disease raises the risk of adenocarcinoma, which can be hard to separate from a focal inflammatory mass. A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic fluid enclosed by a fibrous wall without an epithelial lining, which takes about four weeks to form after acute pancreatitis. It is usually anechoic or contains debris, has a well-defined wall, and most often sits in the lesser sac, though it can track into the mediastinum, spleen, or pelvis. Complications include infection, hemorrhage, rupture, and compression of the bile duct or stomach.
topics.whyLock: Separate the echogenic gland of normal aging from chronic pancreatitis by looking for calcifications and an irregular dilated duct; atrophy alone is not enough. Pseudocysts are named for their missing epithelial lining, a common recall point. Trap: a cystic mass in a patient with no history of pancreatitis should not be called a pseudocyst, because a cystic neoplasm is possible. Trap two: hemorrhage or infection gives a pseudocyst internal echoes, so it can resemble a solid or complex mass; look for posterior enhancement and the absence of internal flow.

topics.title: Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
topics.frontClue: Painless jaundice, a hypoechoic head mass, and two dilated ducts
topics.corePiece: Ductal adenocarcinoma is the most common pancreatic neoplasm and carries a poor prognosis. Risk factors include smoking, chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, and family history; the tumor marker CA 19-9 is often elevated. About two thirds arise in the head. Head tumors present early with painless jaundice and weight loss, while body and tail tumors present late with pain and metastases. The typical appearance is an ill-defined, hypoechoic, solid mass with little internal flow. Head lesions obstruct both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct (double-duct sign) and may produce a large, nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign). The scan must assess resectability and spread: encasement or invasion of the SMA, SMV, portal vein, or celiac axis, liver metastases, peripancreatic and periportal lymph nodes, and ascites. Atrophy of the gland upstream of the tumor with a dilated duct is a secondary sign that a small mass is present.
topics.whyLock: The exam asks you to connect the clinical picture to the location: painless jaundice localizes to the head. A dilated pancreatic duct without an obvious cause should prompt a careful search of the head and uncinate process. Staging questions focus on vessels, because SMA encasement generally makes the tumor unresectable. Trap: focal acute or chronic pancreatitis can also make a hypoechoic head mass, so history and labs matter. Trap two: ampullary and distal bile duct tumors also cause a double-duct sign, so it points to a location, not one specific tumor.

connectionEdges.title: Biliary Obstruction
connectionEdges.link: Head tumors cause distal obstruction with the double-duct sign and Courvoisier gallbladder.

connectionEdges.title: Aorta and Visceral Branches
connectionEdges.link: SMA and celiac encasement determines whether the tumor can be resected.

topics.title: Pancreatic Cystic and Neuroendocrine Tumors
topics.frontClue: Grandmother serous, mother mucinous, daughter pseudopapillary, grandfather IPMN
topics.corePiece: Serous cystadenoma is a benign tumor of older women, usually in the head, composed of many tiny cysts that can look solid or honeycomb-like, often with a central stellate scar that may calcify. Mucinous cystic neoplasm occurs in middle-aged women, usually in the body or tail, and has fewer, larger cysts (macrocystic) with thick septa or mural nodules; it has malignant potential and is resected. Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) is typical of older men and communicates with the pancreatic duct; main-duct IPMN, with a markedly dilated main duct, carries the highest malignant risk, while branch-duct IPMN appears as cysts connected to side branches. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm affects young women and is a mixed solid and cystic mass, often hemorrhagic. Neuroendocrine (islet cell) tumors are well-circumscribed, hypoechoic, and hypervascular. Insulinoma is the most common functioning type and is usually small, causing hypoglycemia; gastrinoma causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and sits in the gastrinoma triangle. Multiple tumors suggest MEN 1.
topics.whyLock: The age and sex mnemonic plus location and cyst size answers most items. Microcystic and central scar means serous and benign; macrocystic in the tail of a middle-aged woman means mucinous and needs surgery. Duct communication is the defining feature of IPMN. Trap: a pseudocyst is the most common pancreatic cyst overall, so history matters, but a septated cyst with nodules is not a pseudocyst. Trap two: neuroendocrine tumors are hypervascular, which helps separate them from the hypovascular adenocarcinoma.

topics.title: Normal Spleen and Variants
topics.frontClue: A round nodule by the splenic hilum that matches the spleen is a splenule
topics.corePiece: The spleen is an intraperitoneal organ in the left upper quadrant, part of the reticuloendothelial system, that filters blood, removes old red cells, and contributes to immunity. Its normal length is usually quoted as up to about 12 to 13 cm in adults. It is homogeneous and slightly more echogenic than or equal to the normal liver, and more echogenic than the kidney. The splenic artery arises from the celiac trunk and the splenic vein exits the hilum to run behind the pancreas. An accessory spleen (splenule) is the most common variant, found in roughly 10 to 30 percent of people, usually near the splenic hilum or tail of pancreas. It is round, smooth, under about 2 to 3 cm, isoechoic to the spleen, and supplied by a splenic artery branch. After splenectomy, splenules can enlarge. Other variants include a wandering spleen on a long pedicle, at risk of torsion, and the asplenia and polysplenia heterotaxy syndromes, often with congenital heart disease.
topics.whyLock: The practical skill is recognizing a splenule so it is not called a lymph node, adrenal mass, or pancreatic tail tumor. Matching echogenicity to the spleen and a vessel from the splenic artery are the clues. Measure the spleen in its longest axis, usually from a coronal intercostal view with the patient in the right lateral decubitus position. Trap: the left lobe of a large liver can wrap around the spleen and mimic a subcapsular collection. Trap two: splenules matter after splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia, because they can cause the disease to recur.

connectionEdges.link: Normal length is the reference for diagnosing enlargement.

topics.title: Splenomegaly
topics.frontClue: Big spleen: think congestion, infection, blood cancer, or storage disease
topics.corePiece: Splenomegaly is generally defined as a length above about 12 to 13 cm, or an inferior tip extending below the lower pole of the left kidney, or a spleen that wraps anteriorly over the left kidney. Causes group into categories. Congestive: portal hypertension from cirrhosis, splenic or portal vein thrombosis, and right heart failure. Infectious: mononucleosis, malaria, bacterial endocarditis, and other systemic infections. Hematologic and neoplastic: leukemia, lymphoma, myelofibrosis, hemolytic anemias, and polycythemia vera. Infiltrative and storage: Gaucher disease and amyloidosis. Massive splenomegaly is classically seen with chronic myelogenous leukemia, myelofibrosis, malaria, and Gaucher disease. In sickle cell disease the spleen may enlarge in childhood and then shrink and calcify through repeated infarction (autosplenectomy). An enlarged spleen is more vulnerable to rupture, which is why patients with mononucleosis are told to avoid contact sports. Echotexture is usually homogeneous, so look for focal lesions, collateral vessels at the hilum, and liver disease to narrow the cause.
topics.whyLock: When you see a large spleen, scan for the cause: a nodular liver and portosystemic collaterals point to portal hypertension, while lymphadenopathy suggests lymphoma. Clinical clues such as a young adult with sore throat and fatigue point to mononucleosis. Trap: an elongated spleen with normal volume can exceed 13 cm in tall people, so use the relationship to the kidney and the overall shape too. Trap two: sickle cell disease produces a large spleen in young children but a small, echogenic, calcified spleen in adults.

connectionEdges.link: Congestive splenomegaly is a major secondary sign of portal hypertension.

checkpoint.reflection: A young child with sickle cell disease has a large spleen, while an adult with the same disease has a tiny one. Why?

topics.title: Splenic Infarct and Trauma
topics.frontClue: Wedge pointing to the hilum is an infarct; left shoulder pain after trauma is Kehr
topics.corePiece: A splenic infarct results from occlusion of a splenic artery branch, from emboli (endocarditis, atrial fibrillation), sickle cell disease, splenomegaly, vasculitis, or hypercoagulable states. It typically appears as a peripheral, wedge-shaped hypoechoic area with the base at the capsule and the apex toward the hilum, without color flow; with time it becomes more echogenic and contracts, and it can be round or multiple. The spleen is among the most commonly injured solid organs in blunt abdominal trauma. Injuries include subcapsular hematoma (a crescent of fluid flattening the splenic contour), intraparenchymal hematoma, laceration (a linear or irregular hypoechoic or heterogeneous defect), and rupture with hemoperitoneum. Fresh blood can be echogenic and nearly isoechoic to spleen, then becomes hypoechoic or complex as it evolves. The FAST exam looks for free fluid in the left upper quadrant (splenorenal space), right upper quadrant (Morison pouch), and pelvis. Left shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation by blood is the Kehr sign. Delayed rupture of a subcapsular hematoma can occur days later.
topics.whyLock: Shape is the key clue for infarct: wedge-shaped and peripheral, pointing to the hilum, because that is the territory of an end artery. In trauma, the exam emphasizes free fluid over organ detail, since CT grades the injury; free fluid in a hypotensive trauma patient is the critical finding. Trap: acute hematoma can be isoechoic to the spleen and easily missed, so look for contour bulges and perisplenic fluid. Trap two: lack of a laceration on ultrasound does not exclude splenic injury.

connectionEdges.title: Splenomegaly
connectionEdges.link: Enlarged spleens are more vulnerable to both infarction and traumatic rupture.

topics.title: Focal Splenic Lesions
topics.frontClue: Tiny bright dots are old granulomas; dark nodules in a big spleen suggest lymphoma
topics.corePiece: Splenic cysts may be true epithelial (congenital) cysts, which are anechoic and may contain thin septa, or post-traumatic pseudocysts, which lack an epithelial lining and often have calcified walls and internal echoes. Echinococcal cysts occur in endemic areas. Hemangioma is the most common benign splenic neoplasm, usually echogenic, and hamartoma is a rarer solid lesion. Multiple small echogenic foci, with or without shadowing, are typical of calcified granulomas from prior histoplasmosis or tuberculosis. In portal hypertension, small echogenic Gamna-Gandy bodies from old hemorrhage can appear. Lymphoma is the most common malignancy of the spleen; it may cause homogeneous splenomegaly or multiple hypoechoic nodules, sometimes nearly anechoic, that can mimic cysts but have no posterior enhancement or have internal flow. Metastases to the spleen are uncommon, classically from melanoma, breast, and lung. Splenic abscesses occur in immunocompromised patients and intravenous drug users, and fungal microabscesses can give a target or wheel-within-a-wheel appearance.
topics.whyLock: Reason by echogenicity and number. Bright, tiny, and multiple means old granulomatous disease and is usually incidental. Hypoechoic and multiple in a patient with lymphadenopathy or B symptoms suggests lymphoma. Near-anechoic lymphoma is a classic trap, because it can look like cysts; look for the lack of a clean back wall and lack of strong posterior enhancement. Fever plus a complex lesion in an immunocompromised patient points to abscess. Remember the spleen is an unusual site for metastases, so a solitary solid lesion is more often benign.

topics.title: Normal Kidney and Congenital Variants
topics.frontClue: Pseudotumors are made of normal cortex; fused poles sit in front of the aorta
topics.corePiece: The adult kidney measures about 10 to 12 cm long, 4 to 6 cm wide, and 2.5 to 4 cm thick, with the two sides normally within about 2 cm of each other. The cortex is hypoechoic or isoechoic to the normal liver and spleen, the medullary pyramids are hypoechoic (especially prominent in neonates), and the central renal sinus is echogenic from fat. Normal variants that mimic masses include the column of Bertin (cortex extending into the sinus), the dromedary hump (a bulge of the left lateral cortex beneath the spleen), and the junctional parenchymal defect (an echogenic triangular notch, usually anterior upper pole). A horseshoe kidney is fused at the lower poles by an isthmus lying anterior to the aorta and IVC, held low by the inferior mesenteric artery, and prone to obstruction and stones. A duplex collecting system obeys the Weigert-Meyer rule: the upper pole ureter inserts inferomedially and tends to obstruct, often with an ectopic ureterocele, while the lower pole ureter tends to reflux. Ectopic kidneys are most often pelvic.
topics.whyLock: The exam often hides a normal variant behind a mass-like description, so ask whether the tissue matches normal cortex in echogenicity and vascular pattern. If it does, it is a pseudotumor. When a kidney is missing from the renal fossa, look in the pelvis and across the midline before calling agenesis. The Weigert-Meyer rule is a favorite: upper pole obstructs, lower pole refluxes. Trap: the isthmus of a horseshoe kidney can be mistaken for a para-aortic lymph node or mass. Trap two: prominent neonatal pyramids are normal, not hydronephrosis or cysts.

topics.title: Renal Cysts and Bosniak
topics.frontClue: Simple cyst: anechoic, thin wall, bright back wall; anything more climbs the Bosniak ladder
topics.corePiece: A simple renal cyst is very common with age and meets three criteria: anechoic, a thin smooth imperceptible wall, and posterior acoustic enhancement. It needs no follow-up. The Bosniak classification, developed for CT and updated for CT and MRI in 2019, stratifies complex cysts. Category I is simple. Category II has a few thin septa, thin calcification, or uniformly hyperattenuating content, and is benign. Category IIF has more numerous or minimally thickened smooth septa and requires follow-up imaging. Category III has thickened or irregular enhancing walls or septa and roughly half are malignant. Category IV contains enhancing soft tissue nodules and most are malignant. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound can characterize enhancement. Parapelvic cysts sit in the sinus and must not be mistaken for hydronephrosis. Polycystic disease includes autosomal dominant PKD (enlarged kidneys with innumerable cysts, liver cysts, berry aneurysms) and autosomal recessive PKD (enlarged echogenic infant kidneys). Dialysis patients develop acquired cystic disease and an increased risk of renal cell carcinoma.
topics.whyLock: Think of the Bosniak ladder as asking one question: how much enhancing tissue is there? More soft tissue means more malignancy risk. On ultrasound, internal flow in a septum or nodule is the equivalent of enhancement. Trap: parapelvic cysts are separate, noncommunicating, and do not connect to a dilated pelvis or ureter, unlike hydronephrosis. Trap two: ultrasound overestimates septal thickness and internal echoes compared with CT, so a complex appearance often needs CT, MRI, or CEUS rather than an immediate diagnosis. ADPKD is inherited and adult; ARPKD presents in infancy.

topics.title: Hydronephrosis and Urolithiasis
topics.frontClue: Connected anechoic spaces in the sinus mean obstruction; twinkling means stone
topics.corePiece: Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces, usually from obstruction. The dilated spaces are anechoic and branch into one connected pelvis. Grading runs from mild (pelvis and calyces mildly dilated) to moderate (rounded calyces) to severe (marked dilation with cortical thinning). False positives include an overdistended bladder, an extrarenal pelvis, parapelvic cysts, prominent renal vessels (use color), and reflux. Causes include stones, UPJ obstruction, pregnancy, tumors, retroperitoneal fibrosis, and bladder outlet obstruction such as an enlarged prostate. Renal stones are echogenic with posterior shadowing; on color Doppler many show twinkling artifact, a rapidly changing color signal behind a rough reflector. Ureteral stones lodge at three narrow points: the ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and the ureterovesical junction, which is the most common site. Ureteral jets seen with color in the bladder suggest at least partial patency; an absent jet on one side supports obstruction. An intrarenal resistive index above about 0.70 may support acute obstruction but is nonspecific.
topics.whyLock: Most stone and obstruction questions combine anatomy and artifacts. Use color to confirm that a dilated sinus is not vascular and twinkling to confirm a stone. Asymmetric ureteral jets are a functional clue. Trap: hydronephrosis may be absent in very early obstruction or with dehydration, so a normal collecting system does not completely exclude a stone. Trap two: check the bladder before calling hydronephrosis, because an overfull bladder can dilate both systems; rescan after voiding. Severity correlates with cortical thinning, which signals chronic obstruction.

connectionEdges.link: Ultrasound separates treatable obstructive renal failure from intrinsic disease.

topics.title: Medical Renal Disease
topics.frontClue: Bright cortex brighter than liver means the kidney itself is sick
topics.corePiece: Renal failure is classified as prerenal (reduced perfusion, such as dehydration or heart failure), intrinsic renal (glomerular, tubular, or interstitial disease, such as acute tubular necrosis or glomerulonephritis), and postrenal (obstruction). Labs show rising BUN and creatinine and a falling glomerular filtration rate. The main role of ultrasound is to exclude obstruction, because postrenal failure is treatable, and to judge chronicity. In acute intrinsic disease the kidneys may be normal or enlarged, sometimes with increased cortical echogenicity. Medical renal disease is suggested when cortical echogenicity is greater than that of the normal liver or spleen, especially with loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Chronic kidney disease produces small (usually under about 9 cm), echogenic kidneys with thin cortex, often with acquired cysts after dialysis. Common chronic causes are diabetes and hypertension; diabetic kidneys may remain normal in size until late. Acute pyelonephritis may look normal or show an enlarged kidney, areas of altered echogenicity, and reduced perfusion; emphysematous pyelonephritis shows gas.
topics.whyLock: Compare cortex to liver at the same depth, and make sure the liver itself is normal, because a fatty liver can make a sick kidney look normal by comparison. Small, bright kidneys mean chronic disease, which means a biopsy is less useful and recovery less likely. Trap: increased echogenicity indicates disease but does not name a specific cause. Trap two: echogenicity tells you little about function; a kidney can look normal in significant acute failure. Always image the bladder and look for hydronephrosis to rule out the postrenal cause first.

connectionEdges.link: Excluding obstruction is the first task in any renal failure exam.

topics.title: Solid Renal Masses
topics.frontClue: Very bright and shadowing suggests fat-filled AML; solid and vascular in a smoker suggests RCC
topics.corePiece: Angiomyolipoma is the most common benign solid renal tumor, composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat. Because of its fat content it is typically very hyperechoic, often as bright as the renal sinus, and may show posterior shadowing. Multiple bilateral AMLs suggest tuberous sclerosis. Larger lesions, commonly over about 4 cm, carry a risk of spontaneous hemorrhage. Because small renal cell carcinomas can also be echogenic, CT or MRI is used to confirm macroscopic fat. Renal cell carcinoma is the most common adult renal malignancy, more frequent in men, smokers, obese patients, dialysis patients, and von Hippel-Lindau disease. Classic triad: hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass, though most are now incidental. RCC is usually a solid mass that is isoechoic or hypoechoic, and often shows internal flow. It tends to invade the renal vein and IVC, so these must be examined. A new left varicocele can signal left renal vein obstruction. Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma arises in the collecting system as a hypoechoic sinus mass.
topics.whyLock: The decision point is whether an echogenic mass is AML or something more dangerous. Brightness similar to sinus fat and shadowing favor AML, but cannot exclude RCC, so further imaging follows. Always follow a solid renal mass into the renal vein and IVC. Trap: Wilms tumor is the pediatric counterpart of RCC, so age matters in the question. Trap two: a hypoechoic mass in the renal sinus splaying the sinus fat suggests urothelial carcinoma rather than RCC. Remember tuberous sclerosis whenever you see multiple bilateral AMLs.

topics.title: Renal Transplant Complications
topics.frontClue: Time since surgery tells you which fluid collection you are looking at
topics.corePiece: A renal transplant is placed extraperitoneally in the iliac fossa, usually the right, with the renal artery anastomosed to the external iliac artery and the ureter implanted into the bladder. Fluid collections are timed: hematoma and urinoma appear early, urinoma typically in the first weeks, lymphocele is the most common, usually 4 to 8 weeks after surgery, often septated, and may compress the ureter causing hydronephrosis; abscess presents with fever. Acute tubular necrosis is the most common cause of early delayed graft function, especially with deceased donors. Rejection may cause an enlarged graft, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and an elevated resistive index (above about 0.8), but these findings are nonspecific and biopsy is diagnostic. Renal vein thrombosis typically shows absent venous flow and reversed diastolic flow in the renal artery. Transplant renal artery stenosis shows high velocities at the anastomosis (often over about 200 to 250 cm/s) and tardus parvus downstream. An arteriovenous fistula after biopsy shows high-velocity, low-resistance flow and perivascular tissue vibration artifact.
topics.whyLock: Sort transplant problems into vascular, collecting system, fluid collections, and parenchymal dysfunction, then use timing. Reversed diastolic arterial flow with no venous signal is the signature of renal vein thrombosis and is an emergency. Trap: an elevated RI does not diagnose rejection; ATN, obstruction, compression by a collection, and drug toxicity all raise it. Trap two: a lymphocele can look like a bladder diverticulum or hydroureter, so trace its connections and check its timing. Mild collecting system fullness is common in transplants and must be compared with prior studies.

topics.title: Bladder and Adrenal Masses
topics.frontClue: A fixed, vascular bladder mass is tumor; a moving, avascular one is clot
topics.corePiece: The distended bladder wall is normally about 3 mm or less, and up to about 5 mm when less full; diffuse thickening suggests cystitis or outlet obstruction with trabeculation. Bladder volume and post-void residual are commonly calculated as length times width times height times about 0.52. Urothelial carcinoma is the most common bladder malignancy, usually presenting with painless hematuria; it is a fixed, irregular wall mass with internal flow. Blood clots and debris are mobile and avascular, and bladder stones are mobile and shadowing. A ureterocele is a cystic dilation of the distal ureter in the bladder (cobra head); a diverticulum is an outpouching with a neck. The adrenal glands sit superomedial to the kidneys; the right lies posterior to the IVC and the left lateral to the aorta. Adenoma is the most common adrenal mass. Myelolipoma contains fat and is very echogenic. Pheochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension and elevated metanephrines. Neonatal adrenal hemorrhage is the most common neonatal adrenal mass, while neuroblastoma is a solid, often calcified childhood tumor.
topics.whyLock: For any bladder mass, ask whether it moves and whether it has flow: tumors are fixed and vascular. Reposition the patient to demonstrate mobility. Adrenal questions hinge on age and lab clues: hypertension episodes with headache and sweating point to pheochromocytoma; a neonate after a difficult delivery points to hemorrhage, which shrinks and changes on follow-up, unlike neuroblastoma, which grows. Trap: a right adrenal mass can be confused with the upper pole of the kidney or the crus of the diaphragm. Trap two: bladder wall thickness must be judged with adequate distension.

topics.title: Aorta and Visceral Branches
topics.frontClue: Celiac seagull first, SMA in its fat collar next, renals off the sides
topics.corePiece: The abdominal aorta enters through the diaphragmatic hiatus and tapers toward its bifurcation into the common iliac arteries at about the level of the umbilicus (L4). Normal diameter is under 3 cm, measured outer wall to outer wall perpendicular to its long axis. The first anterior branch is the celiac trunk, about 1 to 2 cm below the diaphragm, which divides into the common hepatic, splenic, and left gastric arteries (the seagull or T sign in transverse view). The superior mesenteric artery arises about 1 cm below the celiac and runs parallel and anterior to the aorta, surrounded by echogenic fat. The left renal vein passes between the SMA and aorta to reach the IVC; compression there is the nutcracker phenomenon. The renal arteries arise laterally, just below the SMA; the right renal artery passes posterior to the IVC. The celiac trunk and renal arteries have low-resistance flow with continuous diastolic flow. The fasting SMA is high resistance, often triphasic, and becomes low resistance after a meal.
topics.whyLock: Branch order and the waveform logic behind it are the core tested facts. Organs that need constant flow, such as the liver, spleen, and kidneys, are fed by low-resistance arteries; the fasting bowel does not, so the SMA is high resistance until a meal opens up the mesenteric bed. Trap: the right renal artery, not the left renal vein, runs behind the IVC. Trap two: measure the aorta perpendicular to the vessel, not the body, since a tortuous aorta measured obliquely looks falsely enlarged. Use these landmarks to find the pancreas.

topics.title: Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection
topics.frontClue: 3 cm makes it an aneurysm; 5.5 cm in a man usually means repair
topics.corePiece: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is an aortic diameter of 3 cm or more, or at least 1.5 times the normal proximal diameter. Most are infrarenal, fusiform, and atherosclerotic; saccular aneurysms are focal outpouchings and more often mycotic or post-traumatic. US screening guidelines recommend a one-time ultrasound for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked. Measure outer wall to outer wall in the true transverse plane, document the relationship to the renal arteries, the maximum diameter, and iliac extension. Rupture risk rises with size; elective repair is commonly considered at about 5.5 cm in men (about 5.0 cm in women), with rapid growth (about 1 cm per year), or with symptoms. After endovascular repair, ultrasound surveillance looks for sac growth and endoleaks, of which type II, from lumbar arteries or the IMA, is the most common. Dissection shows a mobile intimal flap separating a true lumen, usually smaller with systolic forward flow, from a false lumen that may thrombose.
topics.whyLock: Measurement technique is the heart of AAA questions: outer to outer, perpendicular to the long axis, never including only the patent lumen. Mural thrombus narrows the lumen but not the aneurysm. Trap: a tortuous aorta measured obliquely overestimates diameter. Trap two: a negative ultrasound does not exclude rupture, because retroperitoneal blood is hard to see; a hypotensive patient with a known AAA and back pain is an emergency. In dissection, Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta and needs surgery, while type B begins distal to the left subclavian.

topics.title: IVC and Hepatic Veins
topics.frontClue: The IVC breathes with the patient; a fat, still IVC means the right heart is backed up
topics.corePiece: The IVC lies to the right of the aorta, receives the renal veins and hepatic veins, and enters the right atrium. It is thin walled and changes caliber with respiration and cardiac pulsation; it normally narrows with inspiration (sniff) and widens with Valsalva. A dilated IVC that collapses less than about 50 percent with a sniff suggests elevated right atrial pressure, as in right heart failure or tricuspid regurgitation. The three hepatic veins drain into the IVC just below the diaphragm. Normal hepatic venous Doppler is triphasic or multiphasic: two antegrade waves toward the heart (systolic S and diastolic D) and a small reversed atrial a wave, reflecting right heart events. Tricuspid regurgitation and right heart failure produce exaggerated pulsatility with reversal of the S wave; cirrhosis and other stiff livers dampen the waveform toward flat. Budd-Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction from thrombus, webs, or compression; findings include absent, reversed, or flat hepatic venous flow, intrahepatic collaterals, caudate hypertrophy, and ascites.
topics.whyLock: Hepatic venous waveforms are a window onto the right heart, so reason from cardiac physiology: anything raising right atrial pressure exaggerates pulsatility, while anything stiffening the liver dampens it. Trap: a flat hepatic venous waveform can mean cirrhosis, but also Budd-Chiari or extrinsic compression, so check patency and flow direction. Trap two: do not mistake the reversed a wave of a normal waveform for pathology. The caudate lobe enlarges in Budd-Chiari because its own veins drain directly into the IVC and are often spared.

topics.title: Renal Artery Stenosis Doppler
topics.frontClue: Fast at the narrowing, slow and late beyond it
topics.corePiece: Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension, suspected in severe, resistant, or new-onset hypertension and in renal function that worsens on ACE inhibitors. Atherosclerosis, usually at the ostium or proximal segment, affects older patients; fibromuscular dysplasia affects young to middle-aged women, involves the mid to distal artery, and causes a string-of-beads appearance. The exam is performed after fasting, often in the morning with angle correction of 60 degrees or less. Direct criteria at the stenosis include a renal artery peak systolic velocity above about 180 to 200 cm/s and a renal to aortic velocity ratio (RAR) above about 3.5, both commonly used for stenosis of 60 percent or more. The RAR is less reliable when aortic velocity is unusually high or low. Indirect criteria in the intrarenal segmental arteries reflect a significant upstream stenosis: tardus parvus waveform, acceleration time above about 0.07 s, loss of the early systolic peak, and asymmetric resistive indices. Absent flow and a small kidney under about 8 to 9 cm suggest occlusion.
topics.whyLock: Direct and indirect criteria work as a pair. The jet at the narrowing is fast; the flow beyond it is delayed and damped because the stenosis acts like a filter. If the main artery cannot be seen, intrarenal tardus parvus can still reveal a significant stenosis. Trap: velocities from a poorly angle-corrected or angle above 60 degrees signal are unreliable. Trap two: thresholds vary between labs, so learn the commonly taught values and the concept of the ratio, which corrects for overall cardiac output. Young woman with hypertension suggests fibromuscular dysplasia.

topics.title: Retroperitoneal Masses and Fibrosis
topics.frontClue: Lymphoma lifts the aorta off the spine; fibrosis wraps it without lifting
topics.corePiece: The retroperitoneum contains the kidneys, adrenals, ureters, aorta, IVC, most of the pancreas, the second to fourth parts of the duodenum, and the ascending and descending colon. Retroperitoneal masses displace these structures anteriorly, a key sign of origin. Primary retroperitoneal tumors are mostly malignant, with liposarcoma most common, followed by leiomyosarcoma. Lymphadenopathy appears as hypoechoic, round or confluent masses around the aorta and IVC; bulky nodes can surround and lift the aorta away from the spine (floating aorta). Mesenteric nodes encasing mesenteric vessels can give a sandwich sign. Lymphoma is the classic cause, along with metastatic testicular, cervical, and prostate cancer; testicular cancer spreads first to para-aortic nodes near the renal hilum. Retroperitoneal fibrosis forms a hypoechoic, smooth plaque of tissue around the lower aorta and iliac vessels that encases them and draws the ureters medially, causing hydronephrosis, but does not usually displace the aorta anteriorly. Causes include idiopathic (often IgG4-related) disease, drugs, and malignancy. Retroperitoneal hematoma follows anticoagulation, trauma, or rupture.
topics.whyLock: The tested reasoning is location and displacement. Ask what direction structures are pushed: anterior displacement means a retroperitoneal origin. Then separate lymphoma from fibrosis: lymphoma lifts the aorta and can be bulky and lobulated; fibrosis plasters around the aorta and pulls the ureters inward. Trap: a horseshoe kidney isthmus can mimic a para-aortic mass, so trace it to both kidneys. Trap two: testicular cancer spreads to nodes near the renal hila, not to inguinal nodes, because of its lymphatic drainage.

topics.title: Bowel Wall Layers and IBD
topics.frontClue: Five layers, bright-dark-bright-dark-bright, from lumen outward
topics.corePiece: Normal bowel shows a gut signature of five alternating layers from the lumen outward: an echogenic superficial mucosal interface, hypoechoic deep mucosa (muscularis mucosae), echogenic submucosa, hypoechoic muscularis propria, and echogenic serosa. Normal wall thickness is about 3 mm or less in distended bowel and up to about 5 mm when collapsed. Thickened bowel in cross-section produces a target or doughnut appearance, and in long axis a pseudokidney sign; both are nonspecific and seen with tumor, inflammation, infection, ischemia, or edema. Crohn disease classically affects the terminal ileum with skip lesions, causing transmural wall thickening, hyperemia, echogenic inflamed mesenteric fat (creeping fat), strictures, fistulas, and abscesses. Ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum and spreads continuously proximally, mainly affecting the mucosa. Small bowel obstruction shows fluid-filled loops dilated beyond about 2.5 to 3 cm, with to-and-fro or absent peristalsis; the valvulae conniventes create a keyboard pattern. Graded compression with a linear transducer displaces normal gas-filled bowel to reveal deeper pathology.
topics.whyLock: The layer pattern is a frequent recall item, so memorize it as alternating bright and dark starting bright at the lumen. Preservation of layers favors inflammation, while loss of layering suggests tumor, severe ischemia, or perforation. Trap: a target sign in the bowel means wall thickening, not a liver metastasis pattern; context separates them. Trap two: normal collapsed bowel can appear thick, so measure in distended segments. Transmural involvement and terminal ileum location favor Crohn disease; continuous rectal involvement favors ulcerative colitis.

topics.title: Acute Appendicitis
topics.frontClue: Noncompressible, blind-ending, over 6 mm: the appendix is guilty
topics.corePiece: Acute appendicitis usually results from luminal obstruction, often by an appendicolith or lymphoid hyperplasia. Patients have periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant at McBurney point, fever, nausea, and leukocytosis. Ultrasound uses graded compression with a high-frequency linear transducer to displace bowel. The inflamed appendix is a blind-ending, noncompressible tubular structure arising from the cecum, with an outer diameter over 6 mm, and it shows a target appearance in cross-section. Supporting findings include an appendicolith (echogenic and shadowing), wall hyperemia on color Doppler, echogenic inflamed periappendiceal fat, periappendiceal fluid, and point tenderness directly over the appendix. Perforation is suggested by loss of the echogenic submucosal layer, a periappendiceal abscess or complex collection, and extraluminal appendicolith. A retrocecal appendix can be hard to see. In pregnancy the appendix is displaced upward by the uterus. In women, the differential includes ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy, and tubo-ovarian abscess, so the pelvis should also be imaged.
topics.whyLock: Size alone is not enough: a normal appendix can measure close to 6 mm, so noncompressibility, blind ending, and secondary inflammatory signs are combined. Proving the structure is blind ending separates appendix from terminal ileum, which is peristaltic and connects to the cecum. Trap: a nonvisualized appendix does not exclude appendicitis; it is an indeterminate result. Trap two: a perforated appendix may become compressible or decompressed, so look for abscess and fluid. Ultrasound is first choice in children and pregnancy to avoid radiation.

topics.title: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
topics.frontClue: First-born boy, 3 to 6 weeks, projectile nonbilious vomiting: measure the pylorus
topics.corePiece: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is thickening of the pyloric muscle that obstructs gastric outflow. It usually presents between about 2 and 8 weeks of age, peaking around 3 to 6 weeks, more often in first-born males, with projectile nonbilious vomiting, dehydration, and a hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. A palpable olive-shaped mass may be felt in the epigastrium. Ultrasound with a high-frequency linear transducer, often after giving the infant some fluid and placing the infant right side down, shows a persistently thickened and elongated pylorus. Commonly used criteria are a single muscle wall thickness of 3 mm or more and a channel length of about 15 to 17 mm or more. The thickened pylorus produces a target or doughnut sign in cross-section and a cervix sign in long axis, with redundant mucosa protruding into the antrum (antral nipple sign). Fluid fails to pass through the channel over several minutes of observation. Pylorospasm mimics stenosis but the muscle relaxes and fluid passes during the exam. Treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy.
topics.whyLock: The muscle thickness measurement is the most testable number, so measure only the hypoechoic muscle, not the mucosa. Watching over time is crucial: true stenosis does not open, whereas pylorospasm intermittently does. Trap: bilious vomiting suggests obstruction beyond the ampulla, such as malrotation with volvulus, a surgical emergency, not pyloric stenosis. Trap two: an overdistended stomach pushes the pylorus posteriorly and makes it hard to see; placing the infant right side down or decompressing helps. Gas in the antrum can obscure the channel.

topics.title: Intussusception
topics.frontClue: Toddler with colicky pain and currant jelly stool: look for rings in the right abdomen
topics.corePiece: Intussusception is telescoping of a proximal bowel segment (intussusceptum) into a distal segment (intussuscipiens). It most often affects children between about 6 months and 3 years, peaking under 2 years, and is usually ileocolic and idiopathic, related to lymphoid hyperplasia. The classic triad is intermittent colicky abdominal pain, a palpable sausage-shaped mass, and red currant jelly stool, though all three are often absent. Ultrasound is the first imaging test. In cross-section the mass shows a target or doughnut sign of multiple concentric rings, typically 3 cm or more in diameter, usually in the right abdomen or subhepatic region; in long axis it shows a pseudokidney or sandwich appearance. Trapped mesenteric fat and lymph nodes within the mass are common. Small bowel intussusceptions are smaller, often transient, and usually reduce on their own. In older children and adults, a pathologic lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, polyp, or lymphoma should be sought. Treatment of ileocolic intussusception is image-guided air or hydrostatic enema reduction, unless there is perforation or peritonitis.
topics.whyLock: Age and location are the reasoning shortcuts. A large target in the right abdomen of a toddler is ileocolic intussusception; a small transient target in the left or periumbilical region is likely a self-limited small bowel intussusception. Trap: a pseudokidney sign can be confused with a kidney, so look for the actual kidney nearby. Trap two: trapped fluid within the mass and absent flow suggest ischemia and lower the chance of successful enema reduction. Signs of perforation, such as free air or peritonitis, are contraindications to enema reduction.

topics.title: Ascites and Abscess
topics.frontClue: Clean fluid floats bowel freely; dirty fluid with septa and matted bowel suggests infection or cancer
topics.corePiece: Free peritoneal fluid collects in the most dependent spaces: in a supine patient, the hepatorenal space (Morison pouch) in the upper abdomen and the pelvis (rectouterine or rectovesical pouch), which is the most dependent overall. Other spaces include the subphrenic spaces, paracolic gutters, and splenorenal recess. Transudative ascites, from cirrhosis, heart failure, or renal failure, is usually anechoic with freely floating bowel loops. Exudative ascites, from infection, inflammation, or malignancy, more often contains debris, septations, or loculations, with matted or tethered bowel and possibly peritoneal nodules or omental caking. Hemoperitoneum may be echogenic, with clotted blood near the bleeding source (sentinel clot). An abscess is a localized collection with a thick irregular wall, internal debris, possibly gas with dirty shadowing or ring-down, and no internal flow, often with surrounding hyperemia. Common sites are subphrenic, subhepatic, pelvic, and interloop, frequently after surgery, appendicitis, diverticulitis, or Crohn disease. The FAST exam screens trauma patients for free fluid in the right and left upper quadrants, pelvis, and pericardium.
topics.whyLock: Location tells you where to look, and content tells you what the fluid probably is. Always check Morison pouch and the pelvis first for small volumes. Septations and matted bowel are clues to an exudate, particularly malignancy, while anechoic fluid with floating bowel suggests a transudate, though this is not definitive and only fluid analysis is. Trap: a fluid-filled bowel loop can mimic a collection, so watch for peristalsis. Trap two: echogenic acute blood can be missed if you only look for anechoic fluid.

topics.title: Abdominal Wall Hernias and Masses
topics.frontClue: Ask the patient to bear down: hernias move, most masses do not
topics.corePiece: A hernia is protrusion of fat or bowel through a defect, best demonstrated with dynamic imaging during Valsalva or standing with a linear transducer. Indirect inguinal hernias, the most common type, pass through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follow the spermatic cord, sometimes into the scrotum. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through the Hesselbach triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Femoral hernias lie below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein, are more common in women, and have a high risk of strangulation. Other types are umbilical, ventral, incisional, and Spigelian (at the lateral border of the rectus muscle along the semilunar line). Reducible hernias return with pressure; incarcerated ones do not. Strangulation is suggested by thick-walled, aperistaltic bowel, free fluid within the sac, and absent wall flow. Abdominal wall masses include lipoma (compressible, avascular, iso- to hyperechoic with thin echogenic lines), rectus sheath hematoma (with anticoagulation or coughing), desmoid tumor, and scar endometrioma, which causes cyclic pain at a cesarean scar.
topics.whyLock: The inferior epigastric vessels are the landmark: lateral is indirect, medial is direct, and below the inguinal ligament is femoral. A dynamic maneuver is essential because a hernia may reduce at rest and be missed. Trap: femoral hernias are less common than inguinal hernias even in women, yet carry the higher strangulation risk. Trap two: a rectus sheath hematoma below the arcuate line can cross the midline because the posterior sheath is absent there. Cyclic pain at a cesarean scar points to endometrioma rather than hernia.

topics.title: Thyroid Anatomy and Thyroiditis
topics.frontClue: Hashimoto is heterogeneous and dark; Graves is big and on fire
topics.corePiece: The thyroid has two lobes joined by an isthmus anterior to the trachea; each lobe is about 4 to 6 cm long and up to about 2 cm in anteroposterior and transverse dimensions. Normal parenchyma is homogeneous and more echogenic than the strap muscles anteriorly and the longus colli posteriorly. The common carotid artery and internal jugular vein lie lateral to each lobe, and the esophagus may be seen posterior to the left lobe, where it can mimic a nodule. A pyramidal lobe may arise from the isthmus. Hashimoto thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions, produces an enlarged or later small gland with heterogeneous, hypoechoic, micronodular texture and echogenic fibrous septa; vascularity varies. It raises the risk of thyroid lymphoma. Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism with a diffusely enlarged, often hypoechoic gland and marked hypervascularity (thyroid inferno) with high velocities. Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and causes a tender gland with patchy, ill-defined hypoechoic areas and reduced flow.
topics.whyLock: Thyroiditis questions combine labs, symptoms, and Doppler. High vascularity with hyperthyroidism points to Graves; painful gland after a viral illness with low flow points to subacute thyroiditis; heterogeneous micronodular gland with hypothyroidism points to Hashimoto. Trap: the esophagus behind the left lobe can be mistaken for a nodule; ask the patient to swallow. Trap two: a thyroid inferno can also occur early in Hashimoto, so clinical context matters. Background thyroiditis makes nodule assessment harder because pseudonodules are common.

topics.title: Thyroid Nodules and TI-RADS
topics.frontClue: Add the points: solid, very dark, taller than wide, irregular, punctate foci
topics.corePiece: ACR TI-RADS scores a nodule in five feature groups and adds the points. Composition: cystic or spongiform 0, mixed cystic and solid 1, solid or almost completely solid 2. Echogenicity: anechoic 0, hyperechoic or isoechoic 1, hypoechoic 2, very hypoechoic 3. Shape: wider than tall 0, taller than wide 3. Margin: smooth or ill-defined 0, lobulated or irregular 2, extrathyroidal extension 3. Echogenic foci: none or large comet-tail artifacts 0, macrocalcifications 1, peripheral rim calcifications 2, punctate echogenic foci 3 (points in this category are added for each type present). Total points set the level: TR1 0 points benign, TR2 2 points not suspicious, TR3 3 points mildly suspicious, TR4 4 to 6 moderately suspicious, TR5 7 or more highly suspicious. FNA thresholds are 2.5 cm for TR3, 1.5 cm for TR4, and 1 cm for TR5, with follow-up for smaller nodules at 1.5, 1.0, and 0.5 cm respectively. Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, often solid, hypoechoic, with punctate echogenic foci.
topics.whyLock: Most TI-RADS questions are scoring exercises, so practice adding points from a verbal description. Size thresholds only apply after the level is set. Trap: large comet-tail artifacts in a cystic nodule indicate colloid and score zero, whereas punctate echogenic foci without comet tails score three. Trap two: taller than wide is assessed in the transverse plane only. A spongiform nodule is benign and scores zero for composition, and the other features should not be added on top of it. Very hypoechoic means darker than strap muscle, not just darker than thyroid.

topics.title: Parathyroid, Neck Nodes and Salivary Glands
topics.frontClue: Oval, hypoechoic, behind the thyroid with a polar artery: parathyroid adenoma
topics.corePiece: There are usually four parathyroid glands posterior to the thyroid; normal glands are too small to see. A parathyroid adenoma, the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism with high calcium and parathyroid hormone, is an oval, homogeneous, hypoechoic mass posterior or inferior to the thyroid, separated from it by an echogenic line, often with a polar feeding artery. Normal cervical lymph nodes are oval with an echogenic fatty hilum and hilar flow. Suspicious nodes are round (short-to-long axis ratio above about 0.5), lose the fatty hilum, show peripheral or chaotic flow, or contain microcalcifications or cystic change, features typical of papillary thyroid carcinoma metastases. The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland, drained by the Stensen duct; the submandibular gland, drained by the Wharton duct, is the most common site of salivary stones. Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary tumor, usually parotid; Warthin tumor is the second most common, often in older male smokers, and can be bilateral. Sialadenitis causes an enlarged hypoechoic hypervascular gland.
topics.whyLock: For a posterior neck lesion, decide whether it is thyroid, parathyroid, or node. The echogenic line separating it from the thyroid and a polar artery favor parathyroid; an echogenic hilum favors a benign node. Trap: a posterior thyroid nodule can mimic an adenoma, so look for the separating capsule. Trap two: loss of the fatty hilum in a reactive node can occur, so combine several features. Submandibular stones are more common than parotid stones because Wharton duct secretions are thicker and flow uphill.

topics.title: Acute Scrotum
topics.frontClue: Teen with sudden pain and no flow: torsion; adult with hyperemic epididymis: epididymitis
topics.corePiece: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord, most common in adolescents and often related to a bell-clapper deformity, in which the testis lacks normal posterior fixation. It presents with sudden severe pain, nausea, and an absent cremasteric reflex. Ultrasound shows absent or reduced intratesticular flow compared with the normal side, an enlarged testis that becomes heterogeneous and hypoechoic with time, and a twisted spermatic cord (whirlpool sign). Doppler should be optimized for slow flow (low PRF, low wall filter, appropriate gain) and always compared with the contralateral testis. Partial torsion or spontaneous detorsion may leave some flow. Salvage is high within about 6 hours and falls sharply after 12 to 24 hours, so this is a surgical emergency. Epididymitis is the most common cause of acute scrotal pain in adults; the epididymis, especially the head, is enlarged, hypoechoic, and hyperemic, with reactive hydrocele and wall thickening. Spread to the testis (orchitis) makes it hyperemic. Torsion of the appendix testis affects prepubertal boys, with a small avascular nodule.
topics.whyLock: Doppler comparison is everything: decreased flow is torsion, increased flow is inflammation. Always set slow-flow settings on the normal side first, then compare. Trap: flow does not exclude torsion, because partial or intermittent torsion may preserve some signal, so a twisted cord or asymmetry still matters. Trap two: rebound hyperemia after spontaneous detorsion can mimic orchitis. Time from symptom onset guides urgency, and imaging must not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high.

topics.title: Testicular Masses and Varicocele
topics.frontClue: Inside the testis assume cancer; outside the testis assume benign
topics.corePiece: A solid intratesticular mass is considered malignant until proven otherwise, and most are germ cell tumors. Seminoma is the most common pure germ cell tumor, peaking in the fourth decade, and appears as a homogeneous hypoechoic mass. Nonseminomatous and mixed tumors occur in younger men and are heterogeneous with cystic areas and calcifications. Tumor markers include AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH. Lymphoma is the most common testicular tumor in men over about 60 and is often bilateral. Extratesticular masses are usually benign: epididymal cysts and spermatoceles, hydroceles, and the adenomatoid tumor, the most common extratesticular neoplasm. Testicular microlithiasis shows tiny nonshadowing echogenic foci, commonly defined as five or more per image. A varicocele is dilation of the pampiniform plexus veins above about 2 to 3 mm with reflux during Valsalva. It is left sided in most cases because the left gonadal vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein. A new right-sided or nondecompressing varicocele should prompt a search for an abdominal mass.
topics.whyLock: Location is the first branch point: intratesticular solid means likely cancer and urology referral; extratesticular cystic means likely benign. Then use age: seminoma in the thirties, nonseminoma in the twenties, lymphoma after sixty. Trap: a varicocele can be missed if the patient is not scanned with Valsalva or standing. Trap two: an isolated right varicocele is unusual because the right gonadal vein drains obliquely into the IVC, so it may indicate a mass. Testicular cancer spreads first to retroperitoneal nodes near the renal hila.
