topics.title: Prostate Basics
topics.frontClue: Cancer starts in the peripheral zone; BPH grows in the transition zone
topics.corePiece: The prostate lies below the bladder, surrounding the proximal urethra, and is evaluated transabdominally through a full bladder or more accurately by transrectal ultrasound. The zonal anatomy includes the peripheral zone, which forms about 70 percent of the glandular tissue in young men and gives rise to about 70 percent of prostate cancers; the transition zone, around the urethra, which is the site of benign prostatic hyperplasia; and the central zone, around the ejaculatory ducts. The seminal vesicles lie posterior and superior to the gland. Normal gland weight is about 20 to 25 grams, and volume is estimated with the ellipsoid formula, length times width times height times about 0.52. Benign prostatic hyperplasia enlarges the transition zone, often with calcifications and nodules, and can elevate the bladder base, causing bladder outlet obstruction, a thick trabeculated bladder wall, and increased post-void residual. Prostate cancer may appear as a hypoechoic peripheral zone lesion, but many are isoechoic, so ultrasound is mainly used to guide biopsy. PSA is the screening blood test.
topics.whyLock: Zonal anatomy is the most frequently tested prostate fact: peripheral zone for cancer, transition zone for BPH. Transabdominal scans in the abdomen exam mainly show gland size and its effect on the bladder. Trap: many prostate cancers are isoechoic and invisible on ultrasound, so a normal-looking gland does not exclude cancer. Trap two: an enlarged median lobe can project into the bladder and mimic a bladder mass; trace it to the prostate. The volume formula is the same one used for the bladder and other organs.

topics.title: Patient Preparation and Infection Control
topics.frontClue: NPO for the gallbladder, full bladder for the pelvis, clean hands for everyone
topics.corePiece: Adult abdominal and gallbladder exams usually require fasting for about 6 to 8 hours to distend the gallbladder and reduce bowel gas. Aorta and mesenteric or renal artery Doppler studies are also performed fasting, often in the morning. Renal exams usually need no fasting, but a full bladder helps evaluate the bladder and distal ureters, and pelvic exams use a full bladder as a window. Standard precautions apply to every patient, and hand hygiene before and after contact is the single most important infection-control measure. Alcohol hand rub is not reliable against Clostridioides difficile spores, so soap and water are used. Transmission-based precautions add contact (gown and gloves, as for MRSA or C. difficile), droplet (surgical mask), or airborne (N95 respirator and negative-pressure room, as for tuberculosis) measures. Under the Spaulding classification, transducers on intact skin are noncritical and need low-level disinfection; endocavitary probes on mucous membranes are semicritical and need high-level disinfection plus a probe cover; procedures through broken skin require a sterile cover and sterile gel.
topics.whyLock: Preparation questions test the reason behind each instruction: fasting distends the gallbladder and reduces gas; a full bladder displaces bowel and creates a window. Infection questions test matching: precaution type to organism, and disinfection level to probe use. Trap: a probe cover does not replace high-level disinfection for endocavitary transducers. Trap two: gloves do not replace hand hygiene. A nonfasting patient with a contracted gallbladder should be rescheduled or documented, not reported as abnormal.

topics.title: Ultrasound-Guided Biopsy and Paracentesis
topics.frontClue: In plane shows the whole needle; out of plane shows only a dot
topics.corePiece: Before an ultrasound-guided procedure, the team obtains informed consent, reviews coagulation status and anticoagulant use, confirms the site, and performs a time-out. Sterile technique uses a sterile transducer cover and sterile gel. In the in-plane (long-axis) approach, the needle travels within the beam and its entire shaft and tip are visible. In the out-of-plane (short-axis) approach the needle crosses the beam and appears as an echogenic dot, so the tip must be tracked carefully. Needle visibility improves when the needle is more perpendicular to the beam, with beam steering or needle-enhancement software. Fine-needle aspiration yields cells for cytology; core biopsy yields tissue for histology. Bleeding is the most common significant complication, and color Doppler helps avoid vessels and check for post-procedure hematoma. For paracentesis, choose the largest pocket of fluid free of bowel, usually in a lower quadrant lateral to the rectus sheath, and use color Doppler to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels. For thoracentesis, the needle passes just above a rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle.
topics.whyLock: Expect questions about safety and visualization. The in-plane approach shows the tip continuously, which reduces the risk of passing beyond the target; out of plane, the dot you see may be the shaft rather than the tip. Steep needle angles are hard to see because sound reflects away from the transducer. Trap: the inferior epigastric vessels run within the rectus sheath, so punctures through the rectus muscle risk bleeding. Trap two: the time-out happens right before the procedure begins, not only at registration.

topics.title: Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Basics
topics.frontClue: Microbubbles stay in the vessels and are imaged at low MI
topics.corePiece: Ultrasound contrast agents are gas-filled microbubbles, typically a perfluorocarbon or sulfur hexafluoride gas in a lipid or protein shell, small enough to cross capillaries. They are purely intravascular (blood pool) agents, unlike CT and MRI contrast, which leak into the interstitium. They are excreted by exhaling the gas through the lungs, are not nephrotoxic, involve no ionizing radiation, and can be used in renal failure. Imaging uses contrast-specific modes at a low mechanical index, commonly under about 0.2 to 0.3, so the bubbles oscillate nonlinearly and produce harmonic signals without being destroyed. Liver enhancement phases are arterial (about 10 to 30 seconds after injection), portal venous (about 30 to 120 seconds), and late (after about 120 seconds until the bubbles clear). Hemangioma shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in; HCC typically shows arterial phase hyperenhancement with late, mild washout after about 60 seconds; metastases and non-HCC malignancies wash out early or markedly. Serious allergic reactions are rare, and resuscitation equipment and trained staff should be available.
topics.whyLock: The key concepts are that bubbles stay in the blood pool and that low MI preserves them. Washout timing and degree separate HCC from other malignancies, and the CEUS LI-RADS system formalizes this. Trap: microbubbles do not cause contrast nephropathy, so kidney function is not a barrier. Trap two: a high MI destroys bubbles, so CEUS images look poor if the MI is left at standard settings. Contraindications are mainly known hypersensitivity to the agent or its components.

topics.title: Scanning Protocols and Measurement Technique
topics.frontClue: Two planes, the right position, calipers on the right walls
topics.corePiece: A complete abdominal protocol documents every organ in at least two planes, with labels for side, organ, and position. Patient positioning changes the window: left lateral decubitus brings the liver and gallbladder down from the ribs and moves stones; right lateral decubitus opens a coronal window to the spleen and left kidney; upright or prone views confirm stone mobility; deep inspiration lowers the liver and spleen. Measurement rules are tested repeatedly: the aorta outer wall to outer wall, perpendicular to the vessel; the common bile duct inner wall to inner wall; the gallbladder wall on the anterior wall perpendicular to the beam; the kidney at its maximal long axis. Volumes of the bladder, prostate, and other organs use the ellipsoid formula, length times width times height times about 0.52. For Doppler, keep the angle of insonation at 60 degrees or less, align the angle correction cursor parallel to the vessel wall or flow, size the sample volume to the vessel, and set the scale to avoid aliasing.
topics.whyLock: Protocol questions reward knowing why a step exists. Two planes reduce the chance that an artifact is mistaken for pathology. Measuring perpendicular to the structure avoids oblique overestimation. Doppler angles above 60 degrees magnify velocity errors, so they produce unreliable peak velocities. Trap: the anterior gallbladder wall is measured because the posterior wall is affected by posterior enhancement. Trap two: incomplete documentation of the whole organ, especially the kidney poles or the distal aorta, is a common protocol failure.

topics.title: Critical Findings Communication
topics.frontClue: Emergent findings need a direct call, documented with who, when and how
topics.corePiece: Some findings require urgent action and must be communicated directly and promptly to the responsible provider, following the ACR practice parameter and the institution's policy. Examples in abdominal and superficial ultrasound include ruptured or symptomatic aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, free fluid in an unstable trauma patient, testicular torsion, hepatic artery thrombosis or renal vein thrombosis in a transplant, emphysematous or gangrenous cholecystitis, and strangulated hernia. The sonographer's role is to recognize the finding, notify the interpreting physician immediately according to protocol, and stay with or monitor the patient as needed; the sonographer does not give a diagnosis to the patient. Communication is usually verbal, by phone or in person, rather than relying on a written report, and documentation includes the name of the person notified, the date and time, and the method. Patient privacy rules (HIPAA) limit who may receive results. If a patient becomes unstable during the exam, such as with syncope, chest pain, or hypotension, stop the exam, call for help, and follow the emergency protocol.
topics.whyLock: Scope of practice is the heart of these questions. The sonographer recognizes and escalates, the physician interprets and decides, and everything is documented. Trap: telling a patient they have cancer, torsion, or an aneurysm is outside the sonographer's scope even if the finding is obvious; the right action is to reassure and escalate. Trap two: leaving a message or relying on the final report is not adequate for an emergent finding; a direct conversation with the responsible provider is expected. Patient safety comes before completing the protocol.
